testRun.title: Worms - Test run
testRun.headlessDescription: Let Worms compete {{count}} times without rendering, as fast as the CPU allows.

guide.welcome: Two worms and a fight to the death - welcome to Worms!
guide.rules: The rules are simple. A red and a green worm start on a 72x40 playing field at slightly random positions. Taking turns, starting with red, the worms move to a new free field. Whoever hits the wall, the opposing worm, or themselves loses.
guide.play: Control a worm in two-player and single-player mode and experience the tactical and strategic challenges.
guide.botIntro: In the Bot arena and Your bots tabs, you can write computer programs that fight in your place. Your first bot can be ready in just a few steps!
guide.step1: Go to the Your bots tab. Enter an epic name for your bot and click Create new bot.
guide.step2: Click Edit to open the editor. The program consists of a think function that is called before every step. The template contains a bot that always moves straight ahead because return dir returns the current direction as the next move. More bot examples follow below. Close the editor when you are done.
guide.step3Title: (Step 3) Challenge an opponent in the arena
guide.step3: Go to Bot arena and select your newly created bot first. Then choose an opponent. Clicking Challenge starts a new match. After a while, you will see the result and a replay.
guide.hurray: (Hurray) You have played your first match with your own bot!
guide.advancedIntro: The challenging part is programming the bots. Your ideas matter more than the code. As long as you can describe your idea, an LLM can help you implement it. This makes Worms suitable for beginners too! You can create up to 20 bots.
guide.technicalDetails: The programs are written in modern JavaScript. Since matches run on the server, a sandbox disables security-sensitive features such as network requests. Each call to think may execute up to one million instructions and use up to 1 MB of memory. During a test run, you can print information with console.log().
guide.examplesIntro: The following example programs give you a feel for bot programming. You can challenge them in the arena.

source.zigzagDirection: Determine your bot's movement direction in a zigzag pattern
source.direction: Determine your bot's movement direction at each step
source.width: Width of the playing field (fixed at 74)
source.height: Height of the playing field (fixed at 42)
source.board: Two-dimensional field; board[x][y] describes the contents at (x|y):
source.boardValues: wall, 0 = free, 1 = occupied by you, 2 = occupied by the opponent
source.directionValues: movement direction of your bot (0 = up, 1 = right, 2 = down, 3 = left)
source.canMove: Helper function: checks whether movement in a direction is possible
source.chooseAlternative: Check whether the direction is free, otherwise choose alternatives
source.keepDirection: No valid movement is possible, keep the current direction
